The third pillar, exploring the training and development ecosystem, is about ensuring a long-term, sustainable talent pipeline. This involves identifying and building relationships with the key institutions that produce qualified professionals for the mining and industrial sectors. In the context of South Africa, the Mining Qualifications Authority (MQA) is a central body. The MQA sets the competency standards for a vast range of occupations in the mining industry, accredits training providers (both public and private) to deliver courses against these standards, and oversees the funding and quality assurance of learnerships, apprenticeships, and internships. For Tread Stone CPM to operate successfully in South Africa, it would be crucial to ensure its internal training programs are aligned with MQA unit standards and to partner with MQA-accredited FET (Further Education and Training) colleges or private providers to recruit new talent. A tender bid that includes a clear commitment to MQA-aligned learnerships for local community members would be viewed very favorably, as it addresses the client's social and labor plan (SLP) obligations. This concept extends globally. In Australia, the TAFE (Technical and Further Education) system is the primary provider of vocational training for artisans, offering apprenticeships and certificate-level courses in mechanical fitting, electrical trades, and fabrication. Partnering with regional TAFEs near major mining hubs can create a direct pipeline of newly qualified tradespeople. Universities with strong engineering faculties are the primary source for graduate engineers. Building a relationship with these universities through sponsoring final-year projects, offering vacation work programs, and participating in careers fairs can help Tread Stone CPM become an "employer of choice" for the brightest young engineers.
